reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents with a red, gritty, or irritable eye with discharge, but crucially with normal vision, a clear cornea, normal pupil, and no significant pain — features that distinguish it from serious causes of the red eye
Bacterial conjunctivitis produces purulent, sticky discharge with lids stuck together in the morning; it is usually self-limiting
Viral (often adenoviral) conjunctivitis gives watery discharge, follicles, a preauricular node, and is highly contagious, frequently following an upper respiratory infection
Allergic conjunctivitis is bilateral and itchy with watery discharge, chemosis, and papillae, often with a personal history of atopy
Redness is diffuse and superficial, sparing the circumcorneal zone seen in keratitis and uveitis
Most cases are managed supportively with hygiene measures; topical antibiotics are used for bacterial cases and antihistamine/mast-cell stabiliser drops for allergic disease
Hyperacute, profuse purulent discharge suggests gonococcal infection and is an emergency because it can rapidly perforate the cornea
reference.pathophysiology: Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the mucous membrane lining the eyelids and covering the sclera. It arises from infection (bacterial or viral), allergy, or irritation. Inflammatory mediators dilate conjunctival vessels (causing redness) and increase vascular permeability (causing chemosis and discharge), while the cellular response produces follicles in viral and chlamydial disease or papillae in bacterial and allergic disease. Because the process is confined to the conjunctiva and spares the cornea, anterior chamber, and intraocular structures, vision and pupil responses remain normal in uncomplicated cases.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination assessing discharge type, follicles/papillae, and preauricular nodes
Visual acuity and fluorescein staining to exclude corneal involvement
Conjunctival swabs for culture in severe, hyperacute, neonatal, or non-resolving cases
Testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea in suspected sexually transmitted or neonatal conjunctivitis
Slit-lamp examination to exclude keratitis, uveitis, and angle closure
redFlags: Reduced vision, significant pain, or photophobia — points away from simple conjunctivitis to a sight-threatening cause
Circumcorneal injection, a hazy cornea, or an abnormal pupil suggesting keratitis, uveitis, or angle closure
Hyperacute profuse purulent discharge (possible gonococcal infection) risking rapid corneal perforation
Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum), which requires urgent evaluation for chlamydia and gonococcus
reference.prognosis: Most bacterial, viral, and allergic conjunctivitis is self-limiting or responds readily to treatment with an excellent visual prognosis; serious outcomes occur mainly with gonococcal, chlamydial, or misdiagnosed sight-threatening mimics.
pitfalls: Labelling any red eye as conjunctivitis and missing keratitis, uveitis, or angle-closure glaucoma
Prescribing topical steroids inappropriately and worsening an undiagnosed herpetic keratitis
Overlooking contact lens wear, which raises the risk of sight-threatening keratitis
Failing to recognise hyperacute gonococcal or neonatal conjunctivitis as emergencies
management: Manage most cases supportively with lid hygiene, cold compresses, ocular lubricants and measures to limit contagious spread
Treat bacterial conjunctivitis with a topical antibiotic such as chloramphenicol or fusidic acid, recognising that most cases are self-limiting
Treat allergic conjunctivitis with topical antihistamine and mast-cell-stabiliser drops alongside allergen avoidance
Treat gonococcal or chlamydial conjunctivitis, including ophthalmia neonatorum, with systemic antibiotics and urgent specialist involvement
Reassess and refer urgently if there is reduced vision, significant pain, photophobia or corneal involvement suggesting a sight-threatening alternative diagnosis
Advise on hygiene and infection-control measures to reduce transmission of the highly contagious viral form
